items.stem: Why do astronomers often express distances in light-years?

options.text: Because cosmic distances are so vast that light takes years to cross them, making kilometres unwieldy
options.rationale: Correct: a light-year is the distance light travels in a year, convenient for huge distances.

options.text: Because a light-year measures time, not distance
options.rationale: A light-year is a distance, despite the name.

options.text: Because light slows down to one year in space
options.rationale: Light speed is constant; this is a misconception.

options.text: Because planets are only a light-year apart
options.rationale: Planets are far closer than a light-year apart.

items.explanation: Correct: a light-year is the distance light travels in a year, convenient for huge distances.
items.provenance: original Mastemy item drafted by an AI agent; no external question source

items.stem: The light from distant galaxies is shifted toward longer (redder) wavelengths. What does this provide evidence for? (Select ONE)

options.text: The universe is expanding, carrying galaxies apart
options.rationale: Correct: cosmological redshift is key evidence for expansion.

options.text: The galaxies are cooling down and turning red
options.rationale: Redshift here is about expansion, not surface colour.

options.text: The galaxies are made only of red stars
options.rationale: Composition is not what redshift of this kind indicates.

options.text: Light is being created inside our telescopes
options.rationale: Redshift is a property of the incoming light, not instrument-made.

items.explanation: Correct: cosmological redshift is key evidence for expansion.
items.provenance: original Mastemy item drafted by an AI agent; no external question source

items.stem: Select TWO statements that correctly describe gravity and orbits. (Select TWO)

options.text: Gravity provides the centripetal force that keeps a planet in orbit
options.rationale: Correct: gravity continually pulls the planet toward the Sun, curving its path.

options.text: A satellite in orbit is continually 'falling' toward Earth while moving forward
options.rationale: Correct: orbit is free-fall combined with sideways motion.

options.text: There is no gravity anywhere in space
options.rationale: Gravity acts throughout space; orbits depend on it.

options.text: Planets move in perfectly straight lines forever
options.rationale: Gravity bends their paths into orbits, not straight lines.

items.explanation: Correct: gravity continually pulls the planet toward the Sun, curving its path.
